story_variants.en:
## Vaathiyaar's AI Chronicle

Vaathiyaar stands before a timeline stretching from 1950 to 2026. "Students, AI is not new — it began when Alan Turing asked 'Can machines think?' in 1950. Let me walk you through the most fascinating journey in computing history."

### The Three Waves of AI

**Wave 1 — Symbolic AI (1956-1990s)**
- Rule-based systems, expert systems
- "If X then Y" logic
- Good at chess, bad at conversation

**Wave 2 — Machine Learning (1990s-2017)**
- Learn patterns from data
- Neural networks, decision trees
- Spam filters, recommendation engines

**Wave 3 — Generative AI (2017-present)**
- Transformers and attention mechanism
- GPT, Claude, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion
- Creates text, images, code, music

### Types of AI

| Type | Description | Example |
|------|-------------|--------|
| Narrow AI (ANI) | One specific task | Chess engine, spam filter |
| General AI (AGI) | Human-level reasoning | Does not exist yet |
| Super AI (ASI) | Beyond human | Theoretical only |

> **Key Insight:** Everything you use today — ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot — is Narrow AI. Extremely capable at specific tasks, but not general intelligence.
story_variants.ta:
## வாத்தியாரின் AI வரலாறு

வாத்தியார் 1950 முதல் 2026 வரை நீண்ட ஒரு காலவரிசையின் முன் நிற்கிறார். "மாணவர்களே, AI புதியது அல்ல — 1950-ல் அலன் டூரிங் 'இயந்திரங்கள் சிந்திக்க முடியுமா?' என்று கேட்டபோது தொடங்கியது."

### AI-ன் மூன்று அலைகள்

**அலை 1 — குறியீட்டு AI (1956-1990கள்)**
- விதிமுறை அடிப்படையிலான அமைப்புகள்
- "X என்றால் Y" தர்க்கம்

**அலை 2 — இயந்திர கற்றல் (1990கள்-2017)**
- தரவிலிருந்து வடிவங்களைக் கற்றல்
- நரம்பு வலையமைப்புகள்

**அலை 3 — உருவாக்கும் AI (2017-தற்போது)**
- Transformers மற்றும் கவனிப்பு வழிமுறை
- உரை, படங்கள், குறியீடு உருவாக்குகிறது

# Traditional rule-based approach
def is_spam_rules(email):
    keywords = ['buy now', 'free', 'winner']
    return any(kw in email.lower() for kw in keywords)

test1 = 'You are the WINNER! Click here!'
test2 = 'Congratulations on winning the science fair!'
print(f'Rules on test1: {is_spam_rules(test1)}')
print(f'Rules on test2: {is_spam_rules(test2)}')
print('AI correctly identifies test2 as NOT spam')

under_the_hood.summary: AI has gone through three engines: hand-written rules that a program applies to facts, models whose numbers are learned from labelled data, and huge neural networks that learn to generate text, images and code by predicting what comes next.

steps.title: Symbolic AI: rules written by people
steps.body: An expert system stores rules like 'IF fever AND rash THEN suspect measles' and an inference engine applies them to the facts it is given, chaining one conclusion into the next rule. It is transparent and exact, but someone must write every rule, and it fails on cases nobody anticipated.

nodes.label: next rule may use the new fact

props.caption: Forward chaining in a rule system

steps.title: Machine learning: rules learned from data
steps.body: Instead of writing the spam rule, give a model 10,000 emails labelled spam or not. Training adjusts weights, say +2.1 for 'free' and +1.4 for a link, until predictions match the labels. The 'rules' become numbers found by optimisation, and they adapt when you retrain on new data.

left.label: Symbolic
left.code:
IF 'free' AND link THEN spam
written by a person

right.label: Learned
right.code:
score = 2.1*free + 1.4*link - 3.0
numbers found from labelled data

props.caption: The same spam idea, two engines

steps.title: Deep learning: features learned too
steps.body: Classic ML still needed people to design features. Deep neural networks learn their own features in layers, edges then shapes then objects for images. The 2012 ImageNet result (AlexNet), trained on GPUs, showed how far this could go when data and compute were large enough.

steps.title: Generative AI: predicting the next piece
steps.body: The 2017 transformer made it practical to train very large models on huge amounts of text. Trained only to predict the next token, they learned to write, summarise, translate and code. Image generators apply related ideas to pixels, for example by learning to remove noise step by step.

steps.title: Narrow systems, broad interfaces
steps.body: Every system so far is narrow AI: it does what its training or rules cover. Language models feel general because language can describe many tasks, but they still have no goals of their own and make mistakes outside their data. Artificial general intelligence remains a research goal, not a shipped product.

under_the_hood.takeaway: The history of AI is a shift in where the knowledge comes from: from rules people write, to parameters learned from data, to very large models that learn representations themselves. Each shift traded transparency for flexibility.
